status_summary: The coordination half has been resolved by a court rather than by legislation or an FEC rule. On 2026-06-30 the Supreme Court held in NRSC v. FEC (No. 24-621), 6 to 3, that FECA's limits on party coordinated expenditures violate the First Amendment and that Colorado Republican II no longer stands; the government agreed with the challengers that the limits were unconstitutional. The contribution-limit half has not moved: the FEC's 2026 inflation notice (published 2026-03-03) indexes the coordinated expenditure limits and the lobbyist bundling threshold under existing law, and no statute raising contribution limits or indexing other reporting thresholds was found. The opinion treats base contribution limits as valid anti-circumvention tools and leaves them in place; commentary after the ruling says other limits could face later challenges. On 2026-09-03 the D.D.C. dismissed DCCC v. FEC, holding the claims based on the coordinated expenditure limits moot after the ruling; no FEC rulemaking or guidance after 2026-06-30 was found (the Federal Register lists no FEC documents since that date) and the FEC has lacked a quorum since 2025-05-01.

timeline.event: FEC publishes its annual price index notice setting 2026 coordinated party expenditure limits and the lobbyist bundling threshold under existing statutory indexing; a footnote says the Supreme Court is considering the limits' constitutionality in NRSC v. FEC.

The Court notes the government agreed with the challengers.

timeline.event: Judge Randolph Moss (D.D.C.), in DCCC v. FEC (No. 24-cv-2935), grants the FEC's and the NRSC's motions to dismiss a challenge to the FEC's 2024 closeout of an advisory opinion request on joint-fundraising ads, holding the claims based on the coordinated expenditure limits moot after the Supreme Court's NRSC v. FEC ruling and the remaining disclosure-based claim outside the court's jurisdiction for lack of traceability and redressability; the opinion states that the NRSC ruling did not alter FECA's reporting requirements.

uncertainties: The vote and holding come from the opinion's syllabus page; the full opinion and dissent were not read. The progress number is a judgment: the coordination half is done by judicial holding, the contribution-limit half is not started. Bills to raise contribution limits or index reporting thresholds were not searched in depth, and no FEC rulemaking after the ruling was checked. The administration's role was limited to the government's litigation position as reported in the syllabus. Freshness pass 2026-10-16: the Federal Register API returned no FEC documents since 2026-06-30; the FEC press-release list (newest 2026-10-01) showed only the 2026-06-30 notice of the opinion; the FEC commissioners page lists two members, so no commission votes on guidance are possible. One web search for federal bills raising contribution limits found only law-firm and state-level commentary, so a bill cannot be fully excluded. The FEC press release text was read only in part. Independent review 2026-10-16: the Supreme Court opinion's syllabus (6 to 3, Kavanaugh; Colorado II overruled; base limits left in place; reversed and remanded) and the 2026-09-03 D.D.C. memorandum opinion were opened. The law-firm analysis of 2026-06-30 was moved from the timeline to sources because commentary is not a government action. The FEC quorum statement is sourced to the FEC statement of 2026-04-30 used in sibling record c29-02; the commissioners page listing two members was read by the researcher on 2026-10-16. Progress reflects a judgment that a binding holding removing one of the two recommended changes is partly operative; whether a court ruling should count at all toward a recommendation addressed to Congress and the FEC is a classification choice.
